record.text_content: Seneca, On Providence 5.1. Seneca addresses the objection: 'Why does God allow anything bad to happen to good men?' He answers that God in fact allows nothing bad to happen to them. Crimes and scandals, evil thoughts and greedy plans, blind lust, and avarice directed against another's goods -- God has kept all these far from the good. Whoever demands that God also protect them from what are merely indifferent things misunderstands the divine plan.

record.text_content: 62. After these things, Celsus, wanting to liken the conversion (epistrophe) of sinners from their sins to the sound and noble doctrines among the Greeks -- not to what is done in the mysteries of Mithras or Sabazius or in Hecate's rites or in any other such rituals -- asserts something of the following sort. And let us see what he says, and what we reply. He says: 'An analogy might be drawn with one who promised to heal bodies and then advised people: stay away from doctors and follow me! I shall heal you better than any doctor.' What, then, shall we say to this? That the Christian teaching says: 'Come, all you who are sick, not to a physician who will corrupt you, but to one who heals differently.' For the common physicians among the pagans are like those who 'make the wound worse' (as Scripture says), who apply their so-called cures only to the body while the soul continues to be ruined by the very things the body indulges in. But the true physician cures both soul and body together. And this too I note: that even Celsus himself does not deny that conversions (metanoiai) from the worst wickedness have occurred among those who accepted the word of God; only he belittles these and says they do not last. But I know of many who, having been converted, continue steadfastly to this day in the improved life.

record.text_content: 63. Celsus then makes another comparison, saying: 'Suppose that someone, while offering to teach philosophy, began by proclaiming: let whoever is ignorant come to me, whoever is foolish, whoever is a child; and these I shall make wise.' But no wise man in charge of teaching would speak this way; rather he would say: 'Let whoever is already educated come to me, that I may bring him to a higher level.' Yet it is characteristic of a certain divine generosity that the word of God says both things: 'Let the mature come for mature instruction,' and also: 'Let the sick come for healing.' For the religion (threskeia) established by Jesus does not exclude the uneducated, since it calls them to be healed and progressively improved; and yet it does not exclude the educated either, for it leads them beyond their education to a contemplation (theoria) of deeper truths. The word is manifold: to the simple it provides simplicity of faith (pistis), while to the capable it reveals hidden wisdom (sophia kekrymmene). Neither part is despised: neither the simple are abandoned to remain simple forever, nor the wise denied the divine depth. Rather, both are drawn forward together toward the perfection (teleiosis) that is in Christ.

record.text_content: 67. Furthermore, the Jew in Celsus objects to those who have believed in Jesus, saying: 'What made you abandon the law of your fathers? Being deceived by him whom we have just addressed, you were very ridiculously deceived and have deserted us for another name and another life.' To this we reply that we have not abandoned the law of the fathers but have discovered its deeper meaning. For the prophets themselves foretold that a new covenant (diatheke) would come -- not like the one made with the fathers when they left Egypt. Jeremiah prophesied this explicitly. Jesus brought the new covenant, fulfilling the old, not abolishing it. The so-called 'desertion' is in fact a completion (teleiosis). We have not been deceived but illuminated; we have not abandoned but have understood at last. And the 'other name' -- the name of Christ -- was itself foretold by the prophets. It is Celsus's Jew who, by refusing to see the fulfillment of his own scriptures, is truly deceived.

To this we reply that we have not abandoned the law of the fathers but have discovered its deeper meaning. For the prophets themselves foretold that a new covenant (diatheke) would come -- not like the one made with the fathers when they left Egypt. Jeremiah prophesied this explicitly. Jesus brought the new covenant, fulfilling the old, not abolishing it. The so-called 'desertion' is in fact a completion (teleiosis). We have not been deceived but illuminated; we have not abandoned but have understood at last. And the 'other name' -- the name of Christ -- was itself foretold by the prophets. It is Celsus's Jew who, by refusing to see the fulfillment of his own scriptures, is truly deceived.

record.text_content: 70. The Jew in Celsus then says: 'Not long ago -- just yesterday or the day before -- when we punished this man who deceived you, you abandoned the law of the fathers.' The disciples did not abandon the law of the fathers but recognized in Jesus its goal and fulfillment (telos).

record.text_content: 72. Then Celsus says, through his Jewish character: 'If someone predicted to you that the Son of God would come among men, this was our prophet and he was a prophet of our God. Moses wrote these things and so did the prophets after him.' Celsus's Jew here acknowledges that the prophets foretold the coming of someone. We welcome this admission, for it is precisely our argument: the Jewish prophets did indeed foretell the coming of the Messiah (Christos), and Jesus fulfilled those prophecies. The dispute is not about whether someone was predicted, but about who that someone is. We maintain that the correspondence between the prophetic predictions -- about the manner of his birth, life, death, and resurrection (anastasis) -- and the actual events of Jesus's life constitutes a powerful proof (apodeixis) that he is the one foretold. Those who reject him must show another who fits the prophetic portrait; but no such figure can be found.

record.text_content: 73. Celsus's Jew then says: 'What sort of God is this who cannot even convince his own offspring?' By this he means: what kind of God is the Father if he cannot persuade his own people, the Jews, to accept his Son? To this we reply: the same objection could be made against any teacher of truth. Socrates could not persuade all the Athenians; does this mean his teaching was false? record.text_content: 78. Celsus's Jew then says: 'But that we may not seem to leave any of these points unexamined, let us look at what has been taught by this teacher himself.' He then critiques the moral teachings of Jesus, claiming they are not original but borrowed from the Greeks, especially from Plato and the other philosophers. To this we reply: first, even if there are similarities between the teachings of Jesus and certain Greek philosophers, this does not mean they were borrowed, for truth (aletheia) is one, and it would not be surprising if those who sought truth arrived at similar conclusions. Third, the moral teachings of Jesus are accompanied by a power (dynamis) to transform lives that the teachings of the philosophers, however noble, do not possess to the same degree. The proof is in the multitudes who have been converted from the worst vices to lives of virtue (arete) through the teaching and name of Jesus.

record.text_content: 79. Then Celsus brings forward the saying of Jesus, 'Blessed are the poor' (makarioi hoi ptochoi), and says that this was already expressed by Plato in a much better form when he said that it is not easy for one who is exceedingly good to be at the same time exceedingly rich. But the teaching of Jesus about the poor differs in its orientation and depth from anything in Plato. For Jesus does not merely observe a social fact but declares a spiritual principle: that poverty (ptocheia) can be a disposition of the soul, a detachment from worldly goods that makes one receptive to the kingdom of God (basileia tou theou). Furthermore, the power (dynamis) of this teaching has actually produced communities of people who share their goods and care for the poor -- something that Plato's Republic, for all its theoretical beauty, never achieved in practice.

record.text_content: 80. After this the Jew says, addressing Jesus: 'When you were bathed in the river Jordan, you say that something like a bird appeared and descended upon you.' He then asks: 'What credible witness (martys) saw this apparition? Or who heard the voice from heaven declaring you to be the Son of God? No one but you yourself and perhaps one of those who were punished with you.' To this we reply that the witness was John the Baptist, who is acknowledged even by Josephus the historian as a righteous man. John testified to what he saw and heard, and on the basis of his testimony, many believed. Moreover, the events at the Jordan -- the descent of the Spirit (pneuma) and the voice from heaven -- were foretold by the prophets and are consistent with the whole pattern of divine revelation (apokalypsis). The credibility of the testimony rests not on the number of witnesses but on their character, the coherence of the testimony with earlier prophecies, and the subsequent fruits of the life and teaching of Jesus.

record.text_content: 81. Then Celsus's Jew addresses Jesus regarding the prophecies, asking: 'What was the purpose of your descent to earth? Was it to learn what happens among humans? Do you not know everything, being God? You do know, then, but do not correct -- and is it not possible for you to correct by your divine power (dynamis) without sending someone in the body for this purpose?' To this we reply: the descent of the Son of God to earth was not for the purpose of learning, for he already knew all things, but for the purpose of teaching and redeeming. As a physician does not learn about disease by visiting the sick but applies the cure, so the Word (logos) of God descended not to acquire knowledge but to bring salvation (soteria). And the reason for coming 'in the body' was that those who are themselves in bodies might be able to receive the divine teaching through a form they could perceive and understand. The incarnation (sarkosis) is the divine accommodation to human weakness, the condescension (synkatabasis) of infinite wisdom to the limited capacity of creatures.

record.text_content: 9. Celsus then claims that the Christians' teaching about the resurrection of the body (anastasis somatos) is both disgusting and impossible -- that God would not wish or be able to restore a body that has completely decayed. But we say: nothing is impossible for the God who created all things from nothing. If he could create the body in the first place, he can certainly restore it. The seed analogy used by Paul is instructive: 'What you sow does not come to life unless it dies; and what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare seed.' Just as the plant that grows from the seed is continuous with it yet vastly different, so the resurrected body will be continuous with the mortal body yet transformed into an incorruptible (aphthartos) and glorious (endoxos) state. Celsus shows himself ignorant of the power (dynamis) of God and of the philosophical arguments about the transformation of matter, which even the Greek philosophers acknowledge.

record.text_content: 41. Celsus argues that the Jews, in separating themselves from other nations and refusing to worship other gods, have shown arrogance (alazoneia) and contempt for the rest of humanity. But we say: the refusal to worship false gods is not arrogance but faithfulness to the truth. If one has genuinely discovered that the gods of the nations are not truly divine, it is not arrogance to refuse to worship them—it is intellectual honesty. The arrogance would be in claiming to possess the truth while one does not; but if one does possess it, its proclamation is an act of service, not of pride.

record.text_content: 45. On the nature of divine names (onomata): names are not merely arbitrary conventional labels (kata synthēkēn, in Aristotle's phrase) attached to things by human agreement. There is a deeper relationship between names and the things they name—especially in the case of divine names. The Hebrew names of God (such as Adonai, El Shaddai, Sabaoth) have a certain intrinsic power because they express the very nature of the divine being as understood through revelation. To substitute a conventional translation for these names is not merely a linguistic change; it may deprive the name of its power.

record.text_content: 46. Moses and the prophets absolutely forbade the naming of other gods (onomazein allous theous)—not because God is jealous in a petty human sense, but because to name a false god as though it were divine is to introduce a lie into one's speech about ultimate reality, and this lie corrupts worship and corrupts the soul. This is not arrogance but faithfulness.

record.text_content: 16. After this, Celsus introduces the charge that God, according to the Christians, changes his mind and acts inconsistently. He says: 'If God had long known that human beings would sin, why did he not prevent it from the beginning?' But we say that the existence of free will (to eph' hemin) in rational creatures is a good that God bestowed from the beginning. record.text_content: But we should inquire whether the Lord gave the old covenant to them or to us. Hear what Scripture says: 'The Lord commanded Moses to give the covenant to the people on Mount Sinai.' But listen how it was given to us. Moses received it as a servant, but the Lord himself gave it to us, to the people of inheritance, having suffered for our sake. And it was made manifest why Israel did not receive it: for the servant received it, but the Lord himself gave it to us, the people of inheritance, by patient suffering. Now Moses received it as a servant, but in what way? For it says: 'Moses came down from the mountain with two tablets of stone written by the finger of the hand of the Lord.' And he received them, and carried them down to give them to the people. And the Lord said to Moses: 'Moses, Moses, go down quickly, for your people, whom you led out of the land of Egypt, have transgressed.' And Moses understood and threw the two tablets from his hands; and their covenant was shattered, in order that the covenant of the beloved Jesus might be sealed in our heart, in hope of his faith.

record.text_content: Now I want to write many things—not as a teacher but as it becomes one who loves you not to leave out anything we have—for your salvation. Therefore let us be attentive in these last days, for the whole past time of your faith will be of no use to you unless now, in this lawless time and in the coming offenses, we resist as befits sons of God, lest the Black One gain entrance. Let us flee from every vanity; let us utterly hate the works of the evil way. Do not be alone and withdrawn into yourselves, as if you were already justified, but come together and seek together the common good. For the Scripture says: 'Woe to those who are clever in their own sight and understanding in their own presence.' Let us become spiritual, let us become a perfect temple for God. As far as we are able let us meditate on the fear of God and strive to keep his commandments, so that we may rejoice in his ordinances.

record.text_content: You shall love your neighbor more than your own soul. You shall not murder a child by abortion, nor kill the newborn. You shall not remove your hand from your son or daughter, but from their youth you shall teach them the fear of God. You shall not covet your neighbor's goods; you shall not be greedy. You shall not be joined in soul with the haughty, but you shall walk with humble and righteous people. Whatever things happen to you, accept them as good, knowing that nothing happens apart from God. You shall not be double-minded or double-tongued, for double-tonguedness is a snare of death. You shall be subject to masters in reverence and fear as to a type of God. You shall not command in bitterness your slave or maidservant who hope in the same God, lest they cease to fear the God who is over both of you; for he came not to call in respect of persons, but he came to those whom the Spirit had prepared. You shall share everything with your neighbor and shall not say anything is your own; for if you are fellow-sharers in the incorruptible, how much more in the corruptible things? You shall not be hasty with your tongue, for the mouth is a snare of death. As far as you are able, you shall be pure for the sake of your soul. Do not be one who stretches out his hands to receive but draws them back from giving. You shall love as the apple of your eye everyone who speaks to you the word of the Lord. You shall remember the day of judgment night and day, and you shall seek out the company of holy persons daily, either laboring by speech and going to exhort and meditating on the word, or you shall make it your business to praise and reflect on how you may save a soul by your word; or you shall work with your hands as a ransom for your sins. You shall not hesitate to give or to grumble when giving, for you shall know who is the good paymaster of the reward. You shall keep the precepts you have received, adding nothing to them and taking nothing away.

record.text_content: 3a. In order that the type (typos) established in Isaac, who was offered upon the altar, might also be fulfilled. 3b. What, then, does he say in the prophet? 'And let them eat of the goat offered on the day of the fast for all sins.' Pay careful attention: 'And let all the priests alone eat the entrails, unwashed, with vinegar.' 4. Why? Pay attention to what he commanded: 'Take two goats, fine and alike, and offer them, and let the priest take one as a burnt offering for sins.' 5b. But what shall they do with the other? 'The other,' he says, 'is accursed (epikataratos).'

record.text_content: 6a. Pay attention to how the type of Jesus is revealed: 6b. 'And you shall all spit on it and pierce it and wind the scarlet wool around its head, and so let it be cast into the wilderness.' 7. And when this is done, the one who carries the goat leads it into the wilderness and removes the wool and places it upon a shrub called a thorn-bush (rhachos), whose shoots we are accustomed to eat when we find them in the countryside; thus only the fruit of the thorn-bush is sweet. 8a. What does this mean? Pay attention: 'The one they shall bring to the altar, but the other is accursed,' and the accursed one is crowned. 8b. For on that day they shall see him wearing the long scarlet robe around his flesh, and they shall say: 'Is this not the one whom we once crucified, having despised and pierced and spat upon him? Truly this is the one who then said that he was the Son of God.' 8c. For how is he like that goat? For this reason: 'the goats shall be alike, fine and equal,' so that when they see him coming at that time, they may be struck with amazement at the likeness of the goat.

record.text_content: 9a. See, therefore, the type of the cross and of the one who was to suffer, because the type of Jesus appears in the goat. 9b. But why is it that they place the wool in the middle of the thorns? It is a type of Jesus placed for the church (ekklesia), because whoever wishes to take away the scarlet wool must suffer much, since the thorn is fearsome, and one can gain it only through affliction (thlipsis). 10a. Thus he says: 'Those who wish to see me and to lay hold of my kingdom (basileia) must receive me through affliction and suffering (pathos).' 10b. And what type did he establish when Israel was falling? He made Moses stand and stretch out his arms, and thus Israel was again victorious—but whenever he lowered them, they were again being slain.

record.text_content: 10. Consider, O man, his works: the timely rotation of the seasons, the changes of weather, the orderly course of the elements, the regularity of days and nights and months and years, the varied beauty of seeds and plants and fruits, the diverse provision of different kinds of animals—quadrupeds, birds, reptiles, creatures of water both sea and fresh. And mark how providence (pronoia) supplies nourishment for all flesh, and the subjection in which God has ordained that all things should be to humanity, and how he has arranged that all things should be at peace and in obedience, while all things serve him. Should not all this move you, and draw you to know the Creator (demiourgos)?

record.text_content: 11. But you do not believe that the dead will be raised. record.text_content: 13. But you say, 'Show me your God.' And I would say to you, 'Show me your man, and I will show you my God.' Show me, then, that the eyes of your soul see clearly, and the ears of your heart hear. For just as those who look with the eyes of the body perceive the things of this earthly life and discern what is different—light and darkness, white and black, ugly and beautiful, well-proportioned and disproportioned, well-measured or exceeding measure or falling short—and just as in the same way the things that are apprehended by the hearing, that is to say, sharp or deep or sweet sounds—even so it is with the ears of the heart and the eyes of the soul concerning the ability to see God. For God is seen by those who are able to see him, since they have the eyes of the soul opened. For all have eyes; but in some they are covered over and do not see the light of the sun. Yet it does not follow that because the blind do not see, the light of the sun does not shine; rather, the blind should attribute it to themselves and their own eyes. So also you, O man: the eyes of your soul are covered over by your sins and wicked deeds.

record.text_content: 14. As a mirror when it is polished glistens, so must the human being have a pure soul. When there is rust on the mirror, a person's face cannot be seen in the mirror; in the same way, when sin is in a human being, such a person cannot behold God. Show yourself, therefore, to yourself—whether you are an adulterer, or a fornicator, or a thief, or a robber, or a plunderer; whether you corrupt boys; whether you are insolent, or a slanderer, or wrathful, or envious, or proud, or supercilious; whether you are a brawler, or covetous, or disobedient to parents, or a seller of your children. For to those who do these things God is not manifest, unless they first purify themselves from all defilement. Since all these things darken you like a dark curtain that is drawn, so that your sins do not allow your mind (nous) to look upward and see God.

record.text_content: 5. And do not wonder that God made the world (kosmos) out of pre-existing matter. For just as an artisan, when he receives material from someone, makes of it whatever he pleases, so also the God of all, when he receives material from his own creation, fashions what he wills. But a sculptor's material—whether gold or silver or bronze—is not his own creation, but rather belongs to those who supply it. So also the power (dynamis) of God is shown when he takes matter that has no inherent qualities and makes from it whatever he pleases. Just as the spirit (pneuma) of a human being pervades the whole person but is not seen, so also one cannot see God with human eyes; but he is perceived and understood through his providence (pronoia) and his works.

record.text_content: 6. For as the soul in a human being is not seen, being invisible to people, but is perceived through the motion of the body, so God cannot be seen by human eyes, but is beheld and perceived through his providence and works. Just as one looking at a ship at sea, rigged and in full sail, speeding toward a harbour, will undoubtedly perceive that there is a helmsman in her directing her course, so also must one perceive that God is the governor (kubernetes) of the whole universe, even though he is not visible to the eyes of the flesh, since he is incomprehensible. For if a person cannot look directly at the sun, which is but a very small heavenly body, on account of its exceeding heat and power, how shall mortal man be able to face the glory (doxa) of God, which is beyond expression? For as the pomegranate has within its rind many cells and compartments separated by membranes and containing many seeds, so also the whole of creation (ktisis) is encompassed by the spirit (pneuma) of God, and the encompassing spirit is together with the creation enclosed by the hand of God.

record.text_content: 7. If therefore you speak of thunder and lightning, these too are ordered and governed by the will (thelema) of God. And the same holds for the remaining elements. If I call the course of the sun, this too has been made by his ordinance, being his servant (hyperetes). The moon and stars, too, were set in order to serve fixed times and seasons and years, acting as servants (hyperetounta) in obedience to God. These are the signs (semeia) by which God makes himself known. He commands the earth to produce food for the human race; he arranged the course of rivers and springs to give water; he commanded the sea to be contained so that it would not flood the land. And he who administers and provides all these things, and nourishes and governs the world (kosmos)—this is God, and you must fear and believe him.

record.text_content: This chapter records the first commandment given by the Angel of Repentance: above all things, believe that there is one God who created and ordered all things, who made everything from nothing and encompasses all things while himself being alone uncontained and inconceivable. Believe in him, fear him, and restrain yourself from all evil. Keep these things and you will live; and all who observe this commandment and live a pure life will receive great honor. Whoever transgresses and commits evil cannot be saved — for there is no repentance for those who knowingly choose wickedness after receiving this commandment. record.text_content: The fourth commandment, the first part, addresses the question of putting away a sinful spouse. Hermas asks about a wife who commits adultery: should she be dismissed or taken back? The angel answers that a husband must put aside a wife who sins and commits adultery, for if he continues to live with her while knowing of her sin, he shares in her transgression. When she repents, the husband must take her back — but not repeatedly, for there is only one repentance for the servant of God. Because of the possibility of repentance, the husband who remarries after putting away his sinful wife commits adultery; he must remain alone and hope for the return of the repentant spouse. This commandment also applies to a wife whose husband sins and commits adultery.

Hermas asks whether it is a sin to marry again after one's spouse has died. The angel confirms that there is a second repentance for those who sin after baptism, and it should be undertaken quickly before death. Repentance must be sincere and final.

record.text_content: The fifth commandment concerns patience and ill temper. The Angel of Repentance teaches that patience is a great virtue and strong, and whoever possesses it is immovable by evil. Ill temper (ὀξυχολία), by contrast, is foolish and empty, leading its possessor to ruin. The spirit of anger — bitter, violent, short-tempered — works alongside the devil to disturb the righteous and alienate them from the spirit of truth within them. When anger takes hold of the servant of God, the Holy Spirit departs and the unclean spirit enters and troubles the person from within. Therefore one must put away ill temper and clothe oneself in patience and long-suffering. Patience dwells with those who have full faith, but ill temper dwells with the empty and faithless. One must ask God continually for the spirit of patience, for it is a great good and a mighty defense.

record.text_content: The fifth commandment continues with further instruction on anger and its varieties. The angel distinguishes between just and unjust anger. When such anger or irritability takes hold of a person, he acts foolishly, doing harm to himself and to others, and the truth departs from him. If one seeks to overcome this temper, he must be long-suffering and bear with those who provoke him, not retaliating in kind. In all circumstances one must guard the spirit of gentleness, for nothing is more profitable before God than a quiet, gentle spirit.

Whoever fears God and keeps his commandments will prevail over every adversary. One must fear what must truly be feared and not fear what does not deserve fear. Fear of men, fear of social shame, and fear of the devil are all vain fears that lead the servant of God away from righteousness.

record.text_content: The ninth commandment concerns prayer and the avoidance of double-mindedness. The angel instructs Hermas to cast aside double-mindedness when asking for anything from God, for if you doubt whether you will receive what you ask for, your prayers will go unanswered. The double-minded man is unstable in all his ways and receives nothing from the Lord. But the man who is wholehearted in his petition, who asks without wavering, will have his request granted by the merciful God. Therefore, when you pray to God, believe that you will receive what you ask for; do not be double-minded. For the double-minded man is like a wave driven by the wind and tossed about; he honors God with his lips but his heart is far from him, vacillating between trust and doubt. Put away such double-mindedness and ask God with a single, pure heart, and he who is rich in mercy will grant you your request.

record.text_content: The tenth commandment concerns grief and sorrow, warning Hermas to drive away sadness from himself because sadness is the sister of double-mindedness and of irascibility. Grief is more mischievous than any of the other spirits, for it wears out the Holy Spirit and yet it seems to be weak and not very powerful. The origin of grief is either from some desire that has been frustrated, or from an angry thought that has not been resolved. When an unfulfilled wish produces grief, it extinguishes the spirit within the person and instead of acting for God, the person is consumed by self-pity. The angel urges Hermas to clothe himself in cheerfulness, which has God's favor, and to rejoice in it always. The person who is cheerful accomplishes good deeds, but the person who is sorrowful grieves both the Holy Spirit and the community around him. Drive out grief, which serves the devil, and clothe yourself in the cheerfulness that is from God.

record.text_content: The eleventh commandment addresses the danger of false prophets and the discernment of spirits. There are two kinds of prophets: the true prophet and the false prophet. The true prophet has the divine Spirit and speaks truthfully, and the testimony of his life corresponds to the power of his word — he does not seek money, does not use oracles for private benefit, and does not give advice to individuals who inquire. The false prophet, by contrast, exalts himself, loves the chief seat in the assembly, flatters and fawns on the rich, speaks according to what people desire to hear, and takes payment for his prophecies. The test of the true prophet is the quality of his life and the fruits of his ministry. Those who inquire of the false prophet empower him; those who inquire of the true prophet receive guidance from the divine Spirit. One must be especially careful not to test the true prophet or to give credence to the false one.

record.text_content: The twelfth commandment teaches on the subject of evil desire and the capacity to overcome it. Hermas expresses doubt as to whether anyone can keep all these commandments, given the power of evil desire. The angel reproves him for this doubt: those who have the Lord in their hearts can overcome any desire or any temptation; for the Lord dwells in those who believe in him, and he who has the Lord overcomes every difficulty. But those who have the Lord only on their lips while having the devil in their hearts find the commandments hard and say they cannot be kept. This is a lie, for the commandments are given by God himself, who knows the capacity of his creatures and would not give commandments that cannot be kept. Those who are double-minded, who do not have God truly in their hearts, find the commandments burdensome and difficult. The answer is to believe truly and entirely in God.

Why trouble yourself acquiring goods, lands, buildings, and luxury in a city to which you do not belong and from which you will eventually be expelled? Rather, acquire what you can take with you: widows, orphans, the destitute, the afflicted. Serve God in this way, and these deeds will be laid up as foundations in the city that is your true home.

record.text_content: The second parable (Similitude II) concerns the elm and the vine. Hermas sees an elm tree and a vine growing together, and reflects on the meaning of this pair. The elm is barren and bears no fruit of its own; the vine, if left without support, would crawl along the ground and its fruit would rot in the mud. But when the vine clings to the elm, it bears abundant fruit both for itself and for the tree that supports it. In this way, the wealthy person who appears barren and useless before God is in fact the support of the poor person who prays unceasingly. The poor person, supported and sustained by the generosity of the wealthy, prays for the rich benefactor before God, and those prayers are received as righteous intercession. Thus they assist one another: the wealthy by providing material support, the poor by offering prayer. Neither is complete without the other, and both are rendered fruitful by their mutual cooperation.

So too in this present world, the righteous and the unrighteous cannot be clearly distinguished; in times of prosperity and ease, both appear alike. Their true nature will be revealed only in the age to come, when the Lord appears and judges. Just as in spring the living tree puts forth leaves and blossoms and fruit while the dead tree stands bare, revealing their true nature, so in the coming age the just will be distinguished from the unjust by the verdant fruit of their lives. Therefore do not be dismayed if in this world the righteous and the wicked seem to live in equal comfort; the final judgment will make all things plain. Hermas is exhorted to put aside doubt and to live according to the commandments, trusting in the ultimate justice of God.

record.text_content: The fifth parable (Similitude V), first part, presents the parable of the vineyard and the slave entrusted with fasting. A wealthy man possesses a vineyard and entrusts its care to his slave while he goes on a long journey abroad. He commands the slave to build a fence around the vineyard and gives him no further instruction. The faithful slave not only fulfills what was commanded but goes beyond: he digs up the vineyard, removes the weeds, tends the vines, and prepares it far better than expected. When the master returns and sees the slave's excellent and exceeding service, he rewards him lavishly — granting him his freedom, including him as a co-heir with his own son, and sharing the feast with him along with his friends. The slave's extraordinary diligence and willingness to exceed the minimum requirement of the commandment serves as a model for the Christian's life of fasting and righteous deeds that go beyond what is merely obligatory.

record.text_content: The fifth parable continues with the allegorical interpretation. The explanation is extended to the nature of the Son of God's relationship with the Holy Spirit: the holy pre-existent Spirit, which dwelt in the flesh of Christ and through which he labored and did all good works, was rewarded by the Father. The flesh that served the Spirit faithfully and without defilement was taken up into the glory of the Spirit. Hermas is taught that all who defile the flesh — which is the temple of the Spirit — will not receive salvation, for the defilement of the holy vessel is an irreparable injury.

record.text_content: The fifth parable, third section, discusses the relationship between fasting and righteous action. Hermas is taught that the fast God truly accepts is not merely the abstinence from food, but the keeping of the commandments and the performance of righteous deeds in place of the food one has foregone. On the day you fast, count what you would have spent on food; set that amount aside and give it to a widow, an orphan, or a person in want. This is the kind of fasting that is holy and pure and that the Lord accepts. If you fulfill the commandments in this manner and do not pursue luxury but care instead for those who suffer, you will live before God. One must not fast externally while internally harboring evil. The fast of the soul consists in not committing evil; the fast of the body, in setting aside food and directing its cost to the service of those in need. Both together constitute the fast acceptable to God.

record.text_content: The sixth parable continues, explaining the lengths of time that different kinds of sinners spend under the rod of the punishing angel. Those who have given themselves over to luxury and deceit for a long time suffer correction for twice as long a period; those who have been doubly corrupt are punished doubly. The punishment is always proportionate to the sin and always aimed at redemption. Some endure their punishment without complaint and are delivered more quickly; others resist and murmur against God, and their time of punishment is extended. Hermas is told that the punishing angel is not acting out of cruelty but out of mercy — he is an instrument of God's corrective justice rather than of divine vengeance. The chastisement administered through suffering in this life is infinitely preferable to the punishment in the next, and it serves to restore the servant of God to a condition of penitence and renewal if he endures it with humility and gratitude.

record.text_content: The sixth parable, third section, contains the angel's further explanation of the manner in which the punishing shepherd's operation works. Those who are delivered to the punishing angel are those who have sinned and strayed from the path of righteousness — apostates and those who have given themselves to worldly pleasures in a manner incompatible with faithful service to God. The punishing shepherd drives them over rugged terrain, through thorns and briars, through gullies and swamps, without rest, so that they endure much suffering. This is the purpose of tribulation: it beats down the body and the sinful will and prepares the soul for the return to God. Once the appointed time of chastisement is completed, the guardian shepherd of repentance receives the sinners back and restores them to the green pasture of the righteous. Whoever endures the discipline without apostasizing will be saved; whoever refuses to submit to discipline and flees from the shepherd of repentance will be lost.

record.text_content: The seventh parable (Similitude VII) presents a further vision of punishment and intercession. Hermas sees himself sitting with the angel of punishment watching over a large flock. He is told that the flock under the punishing shepherd's care includes members of his own household. He asks the angel of repentance to intercede that the discipline be lightened. The angel tells Hermas that if he wishes intercession to be effective on behalf of those being punished, he himself must be pure and must refrain from all evil — for it is only from a position of righteous integrity that intercession can avail. The punishment that is being administered to Hermas's household is the direct result of their sins. As long as Hermas himself remains under the influence of evil and does not keep the commandments of God, the shepherd of repentance cannot present his intercession to God. Hermas must first purify himself completely before his intercession can be heard.

record.text_content: The eighth parable (Similitude VIII) begins with a vision of a great willow tree whose branches and shade spread over plains and mountains alike. A large crowd of people has come to stand beneath the tree, and a splendid angel standing beside it is cutting branches and distributing one to each person in the crowd. When all the branches have been distributed and each person holds one, the angel lays down the axe and the tree remains as healthy and full as before — nothing has been diminished. Hermas marvels at this and asks the shepherd what it signifies. The angel of repentance explains that the great willow tree is the Law of God given to the whole world; the magnificent angel who administered the branches is the Son of God, the great and glorious lord of the whole creation; and the diverse people who received branches are those to whom the Law has been proclaimed and who have received it in different ways.

The woman — the Church — cannot yet appear in her full glory because Hermas and his household have not been fully purified. If he will see to the complete purification of his house and the repentance of all within it, the Church will appear to him in all her perfection and splendor. The vision closes with exhortations to Hermas to live righteously and to bring his entire household to repentance without delay.

record.text_content: The eighth parable continues with the examination of the returned branches and the sorting of the people. Those who submitted entirely withered and gnawed branches are found to be apostates and blasphemers who have spoken wickedly against the Lord and betrayed the servants of God; there is no repentance for them, and their death is already determined. Those who submitted completely dry branches are the apostates and traitors who have abandoned the faith without going so far as blasphemy; repentance may still be possible for them, but only barely. Those who submitted half-dry branches are those who are in the world with one foot and in the faith with another — double-minded people who live neither truly for God nor entirely for the world. For these there is hope of repentance if they act quickly. Each category is examined and sorted with scrupulous justice, the angel taking account of the full range of human moral conditions.

The tower is not yet complete; the season of repentance is still open; but it will close, and those who have not repented when it closes will be forever excluded from the building.

record.text_content: The ninth parable (Similitude IX) opens with the angel bringing Hermas to Arcadia, to a place where there is a great plain surrounded by twelve mountains, each of a different character. The angel shows Hermas a large white rock rising from the plain, higher than the mountains. On the rock a gate has been cut, and the gate shines more brilliantly than the sun itself. Hermas marvels at the brilliance of the gate. Six young men — the same builders as before — stand before the gate, along with multitudes of people from the surrounding mountains, each coming to pass through the gate. Those who enter the gate do so only by passing through the gate; there is no other way up the rock or into what lies beyond it. The angel tells Hermas that the gate is the Son of God, the only way into the Kingdom, and no one can enter without passing through him. This gate is the sole means of access to the tower built upon the great rock.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues with further details of the tower's construction. The six builders examine all the stones offered for the building. Those that are round — representing worldly wealth and attachment to material things — cannot be placed in the tower unless their roundness is cut away. The prosperous and wealthy among the people are like these round stones; until they are trimmed of their attachment to wealth and worldly honor, they cannot fit into the structure of the holy community. But once their attachment is cut away and they become humble and simple — like squared stones — they fit perfectly and are placed in the tower. Others come forward with already squared and bright white stones; these are placed directly and prominently in the building, fitting together seamlessly. Those whose stones cannot be squared or refuse to relinquish their round form are placed far from the gate and the tower, left outside in the plain.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues with the revelation of the meaning of the twelve mountains surrounding the plain. The first mountain — black as soot — represents those who apostasized from the faith and blasphemed the Lord; they are servants of sin in every form and are completely dead spiritually. The second mountain — bare and fruitless — represents the hypocrites who profess belief but do not act on it; they seem to be believers but are spiritually empty. The third mountain — covered in thorns and thistles — represents those who believe but are entangled in worldly wealth, business affairs, and pagan associations, so that the fruit of faith is choked out by the thorns of worldly care. The fourth mountain — with plants that are half green and half dry — represents the double-minded: those who are in the world for some seasons and in the faith for others, living in spiritual uncertainty and wavering commitment.

The ninth mountain — entirely waterless, desolate, and full of deadly serpents — represents the deacons who administered the goods of the Church in a corrupt manner, robbing widows and orphans of what was entrusted to them. They will be lost unless they repent. The tenth mountain — covered with great shady trees under which sheep rested and ruminated — represents the bishops who sheltered those in need and those who had gone astray under the protection of their office, always interceding for others before God. The eleventh — covered with fruit-laden trees — represents the martyrs who suffered joyfully. The twelfth — entirely white and gleaming — represents the newly baptized and the innocent who are completely pure.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues with an account of the Son of God inspecting the tower. A great and glorious man, the Lord of the whole building, arrives to inspect the tower. He examines every stone carefully, striking some with a rod. Some of the stones in the building turn black and are removed; some are found cracked and are cut out; some are found too short and are cast away to be reshaped; some are found white but round. These too are removed from the structure of the tower and placed near it with the instruction that they must be reshaped — their roundness removed — if they are to be placed in the building. Meanwhile the Lord calls the twelve virgins and instructs them to carry the round stones and to send them through the gate so that they may pass through the Son of God and be reshaped by the virtues. The gate and the inspection together constitute the final eschatological judgment of the community.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues with the young men removing stones from the tower at the command of the great man. The stones removed are of various types: those that are black, those that are cracked or chipped, those that are too short, those that are white but round. All of these are set aside, and new stones are brought to fill their places — all of them bright, shining, and perfectly squared. The young men then build with these new stones while the cracked and defective ones are cast far from the tower. Hermas asks what will become of the rejected stones. He is told that those that are not entirely ruined may yet be reshaped and placed in the building, but only if they are willing to submit to being cut and trimmed. Those that are completely rotten and ruined — the black ones — cannot be used and are permanently cast out. The message is that even the imperfect may be restored through genuine repentance, but willful hardness of heart makes restoration impossible.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues as Hermas seeks clarification about what the tower means, who the man is who inspects it, and who the virgins are that accompany the stones. The angel tells him that the great white rock and the gate represent the Son of God; the rock is ancient — older than all creation — and the gate was cut only recently, so that the elect might enter through him. All who enter the Kingdom of God must enter through this gate. The tower represents the Church. The young men building the tower are the holy angels of the Lord who were first created. The twelve virgins are holy spirits — the virtues — without which no one can enter the Kingdom; whoever is clothed with them is received into the tower. These virgins are more powerful than the builders themselves, for without them no stone can be set in the tower. They carry the stones through the gate and place them within the tower.

record.text_content: The ninth parable addresses Hermas's question about the name of the Son of God. The angel answers that the Son of God has many names, each deriving from his various works and gifts; but the greatest and most fundamental name is that which he bears by virtue of his pre-existence and his creative activity. Hermas asks for the names and is told that some of them are known and some not. He is given a series of names by which the Son is invoked. The angel explains that those who enter the tower through the Son of God and are carried by the virtues represented by the twelve virgins will be clothed with the power of the Name. Furthermore, Hermas is told why the Son of God appears in human form to those who can see him: it is so that those whom he must guide and protect may recognize him and not be afraid, for if he were to appear in his full divine glory, no mortal could endure the sight.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues with a question from Hermas about those virgins and other young women who stand outside the tower in darkness. Whoever keeps company with these vices cannot serve God and cannot be placed within the holy tower. The two groups of women — the holy virgins and the wicked ones — are always at war for the souls of the servants of God. Hermas is instructed to put on the garments of the holy virgins and to flee from the embraces of the evil women so that he may live and dwell in the tower.

record.text_content: The ninth parable explains why the stones drawn from the deep waters shine so brilliantly when placed in the tower. Hermas asks this question, and the angel tells him that these stones represent those who suffered for the name of the Son of God. They were plunged into the depths of tribulation, suffering, and death, and in that suffering they were purified and whitened; just as gold refined in a furnace comes out purer and brighter, so these righteous persons, tried in the fire of persecution, emerge radiant and incorruptible. They were planted in the foundation of the tower because they are the most steadfast and brilliant of all. Hermas asks whether those who are placed outside the wall near the tower still have hope of entering the tower. He is told that they do — but only if they quickly return through the gate, which is the Son of God, and are clothed by the twelve holy virgins, who will carry them through the gate and place them in the building.

record.text_content: The ninth parable describes the condition and future prospects of the people who came from the various mountains, sorted according to the state of their returned branches. Those from the second mountain who submitted completely dry branches are those who have secretly harbored unbelief despite their outward profession; they are like the dry, fruitless mountain — apparently belonging to the community of faith but in fact spiritually barren. Some among them are still capable of repentance if they act quickly; others have gone so far in secret apostasy that they are virtually beyond recall. Those from the third mountain — the thorny, thorn-covered mountain — submitted branches that were partly green and partly dried and choked; they represent those whose faith is genuine but whose worldly entanglements and moral compromises prevent them from bearing fruit. They still have hope if they will cut away the thorns of worldliness and live simply and righteously.

record.text_content: The ninth parable describes those who came from the fourth mountain, the mountain with half-dry and half-green plants. These believers are double-minded, vacillating between commitment to God and commitment to the world. They are neither wholly righteous nor wholly corrupt, but occupy an unstable middle ground. Many of them do repent when they hear the call to repentance, and when they repent sincerely, their place in the tower is secured. But others among them remain permanently double-minded and never achieve the stability of genuine faith; these are lost because they refused to make a definitive choice. The angel explains that double-mindedness is extremely dangerous — perhaps the most common spiritual disease among the people of God — because it prevents both full repentance and full righteousness, leaving the person permanently in a twilight condition unable to bear fruit for God or to enter the tower.

record.text_content: The ninth parable describes those from the twelfth mountain — entirely white and gleaming — who submitted entirely green, luxuriant branches full of new shoots. These are innocent, newly baptized believers who have always been good, faithful, and honored before God. They sinned in only the slightest ways through minor desires and petty resentments, and when they heard the call to repentance, the greater part of them repented quickly, making their dwelling in the tower. Some few among them were double-minded and created greater dissensions, but even for these there remains hope of repentance given their fundamentally good character; it is unlikely any of them will truly die spiritually. Also described are those who returned entirely dry branches with just a small amount of green: these are the believers who did the works of lawlessness and never truly departed from God; they bore the Name gladly and willingly received the servants of God into their homes. record.text_content: The ninth parable continues with the vision of the tower being built upon the great white rock. Those from the mountains are placed in the upper structure and vary greatly in character. When the building is at rest temporarily, waiting for additional stones from the deep, the great man — the Lord of the tower — arrives with six angels of magnificence and beauty and inspects the entire structure carefully. Hermas is taught that the evil of slander is essentially a form of double-mindedness and spiritual restlessness; those who slander cannot be at peace and cannot be at one with the community of the faithful. The commandment to give generously without discrimination — to give to all who ask — is further elaborated. One must not exercise judgment over who is worthy of charity and who is not; that discernment belongs to God alone. The giver's responsibility is to give, and the receiver's responsibility is to render account to God for what was received. If someone asks in deceit and receives, the giver is not held accountable, but the deceiver will face judgment. The righteous person must be prepared to be deceived occasionally in the exercise of generosity rather than risk withholding from a genuine need out of excessive caution.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues with further description of the people who came through the gate from the various mountains. The large and joyful crowds of people who came from the surrounding mountains through the gate and received white garments from the virgins are the believers from all the nations of the world. After passing through the gate, some go directly to the building and are fitted into it immediately; others are rejected by the builders and set aside. Hermas asks why some who had passed through the gate and received white garments are still set aside from the building. The angel explains that merely passing through the gate and receiving the white garment — that is, receiving baptism — is not sufficient; one must also have the Name confirmed by the activity of the virtuous spirits, the twelve virgins, who must carry and clothe the person fully. Those who passed through the gate but were not carried by the virgins cannot be placed in the building.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues with an account of how stones that are placed outside the tower near the gate can still be admitted to the building. The angel explains to Hermas that those stones placed near the tower but not yet in it — the white, round stones — represent the wealthy who profess faith but are still shaped by their attachment to wealth and worldly status. If they renounce their wealth or if their riches are cut away by adversity, they will be reshaped into squares and will fit into the building. But if they persist in their round, worldly form until the tower is complete and the Lord returns to inspect it, they will be found useless and will be cast out entirely. This is a final warning to the wealthy who have received the faith: they must act now, while there is still time and the tower is still under construction, to strip themselves of worldly attachment and allow themselves to be squared and fitted for the building.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues with Hermas asking about the meaning of the great white rock with the ancient gate cut into it. The angel explains that the rock and the gate represent the Son of God. The rock is ancient because the Son was with the Father from the beginning of creation, as the Father's counselor; but the gate is new, because the Son appeared in the last days in a manifestation that was not visible before, in order that those who are to be saved might enter through him into the Kingdom of God. The gate shines more brightly than the sun because the Name of the Son of God is the most powerful and radiant of all names; it alone can give access to eternal life. No one can enter the Kingdom of the Father without passing through this gate. Furthermore, the gate is the only entry; there is no way to reach the great white rock except through the gate itself, and no way to dwell in the tower except by entering through the gate.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues with the examination of those who submitted stones to the builders from the different mountains. The latter must wait until the tower is fully inspected; if the Lord finds them worthy during the final inspection, they will be placed in the building then. Hermas is also told about those whose branches in the eighth parable bore some green and some dry portions — these are the partially faithful and partially sinful, and the fate of each depends on which portion of their spiritual condition prevails at the end. Half-measures and partial repentance are not sufficient; what is needed is a total conversion of heart and life, an unreserved turning to God.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues with the interpretation of the removal of defective stones from the tower. The black stones represent apostates who have completely denied the faith; they cannot be reinserted. The cracked and chipped stones represent those who believed with their mouths but held wickedness in their hearts; they appear sound on the surface but are fundamentally damaged within. They may still be repaired if they repent completely and eliminate their hidden wickedness. The short and undersized stones represent those who believed but did not grow in virtue; they remained spiritually stunted. These may be made fit if they are willing to be worked on — reshaped by the discipline of the virtuous life. The white but round stones represent the wealthy and comfortable believers who need to relinquish their attachment to wealth. Each category of defect has a corresponding remedy available through repentance, with the exception of the entirely black and ruined stones, which are beyond restoration.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues with the Lord of the tower instructing the builders as to which rejected stones may be restored to the building. All this remedial work requires a period of time during which the person repents and is reformed. The tower will wait for these stones; the building has been paused temporarily, and this pause is precisely the opportunity for the rejected stones to be reshaped. However, the pause is strictly limited; once the building resumes and is completed, no further changes will be made. Those who have not been reformed during this window of opportunity will be permanently excluded.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues with an explanation of the various colors of the stones from the twelve different mountains and what their differences signify. Just as the mountains themselves are of different characters, so the stones drawn from each mountain carry the spiritual character of that mountain with them. This is why some stones fit immediately into the tower and others do not — their spiritual quality is determined by the condition of their source. However, once they have passed through the gate of the Son of God and been clothed in the white garments by the twelve virgins, they receive a new quality that transcends their mountain of origin. The white garment represents the Name of the Son of God, and whoever is truly clothed in that Name — not merely externally but in heart and life — becomes a fitting stone for the tower regardless of the mountain from which they came. The diversity of origin is transcended by the unity of the Name.

record.text_content: The third commandment as given here concerns the absolute necessity of truth as the foundation of the Christian life. God is truth, and his dwelling is truth; those who are truthful in every respect participate in the nature of God and are given a place in his household. Deceit and falsehood, by contrast, are the tools of the devil; those who practice deception remove themselves from God and ally themselves with the powers of evil. The angel instructs Hermas that the servant of God must not only avoid explicit lies but must cultivate a deep, wholehearted commitment to truthfulness in every aspect of life — in speech, in business, in relationships, and in the management of the household. He must be honest even when honesty is costly, for the alternative is to become like those who have no faith and no fear of God. The Lord's servants are recognizable precisely by their love of truth and their rejection of every form of deception and pretense.

record.text_content: The ninth parable addresses Hermas's question about whether those who submitted withered and decayed branches can be restored. The angel gives a qualified answer: those whose branches were slightly green even at their worst — that is, those who retained even the smallest remnant of faith and good intention — still have a possibility of repentance and restoration if they act before the tower's completion. But those whose branches were entirely dead and black, without any green whatsoever, cannot be revived or restored; they have placed themselves irrevocably outside the possibility of repentance through their willful and total apostasy. The distinction is crucial: the presence of even a tiny spark of genuine faith or good will is sufficient grounds for the mercy of God to operate; the complete absence of any such spark means that there is nothing on which mercy can take hold. Hermas is urged to transmit this teaching immediately to all who need it, so that none should miss the opportunity while it remains.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues as the angel addresses the condition of the wealthy in the community of faith. Hermas asks whether the round stones — representing the wealthy — can truly be refashioned into squares and placed in the tower. The angel affirms that they can, but emphasizes the extreme difficulty involved: wealth is like a great weight pressing down on the soul and bending it away from righteousness; it is very hard for the wealthy person to enter the Kingdom of God, but it is not impossible. What is required is a genuine and practical renunciation — not merely an internal detachment but actual generosity in giving away excess wealth to the service of the poor and the community. When the wealthy person does this — when the roundness of accumulated treasure is cut away through active generosity — the stone becomes squared and can be placed in the building. The window for this transformation remains open only as long as the tower is under construction.

record.text_content: The ninth parable continues with a vision of the gate's glorious and powerful nature. The gate shines with extraordinary radiance because it represents the Son of God, who is the light of the world. All who wish to enter the Kingdom must pass through him; there is no alternative route. record.text_content: The ninth parable contains a passage in which the angel explains to Hermas the significance of the fact that the building of the tower was temporarily suspended while the stones being used were drawn from the deep. This suspension represents the present season of repentance: the tower is paused, waiting, because the Lord in his mercy has allowed time for all those outside it who can still be reformed to be brought to repentance and reshaped into fitting stones. The deep from which the most glorious stones come represents the tribulations and sufferings that purify the most faithful; the ordinary stones from the plain represent those who come to faith through the ordinary course of the gospel proclamation. Both kinds of stone are necessary for the building; both are precious in the sight of the Lord. The angel tells Hermas that when the tower is complete and the Lord comes to inspect it, then the ages of this world will come to an end and the new age will begin.

record.text_content: The ninth parable describes the characteristics of those who came from the various mountains and presented stones of intermediate quality. From the mountain representing those who had faith but were entangled in business and worldly affairs, some came with stones that were partly green and partly gray or whitish — reflecting a faith that was genuine but significantly compromised by worldly priorities. From the mountain representing those who bore grudges and created divisions, some came with stones that were cracked but in which the cracks had been sealed by genuine repentance, while others still had visible fault-lines indicating unresolved bitterness. From the mountain of the self-opinionated and presumptuous, the repentant ones emerged with stones that were well-squared and fitted, their arrogance having been trimmed away, while the unrepentant ones remained rough and jagged. The diversity of outcome from similar starting points illustrates the decisive role of the individual's free response to the call to repentance.
